title: The Most Valuable Step in Writing with AI Isn't the Prompt—It's Turning Editing Feedback into Compound Interest
dek: Katie uses AI from career coach to writing plugin: first load the model with context, then save every editing comment back into the system to compound. For her, AI's value isn't just efficiency—it's also a support system that steadies her emotions and helps her get past execution hurdles.
why: Not another prompt demonstration, but a rare look at how one author built her own AI workflow: how to set up context files, how to choose reviewers, and even how non-technical people can avoid pitfalls—all concrete and copyable.
who: Journalists and editors producing content, writing public accounts, or long-form pieces, as well as independent developers building AI as a personal productivity system; especially those stuck with homogeneous AI output and wanting to establish their own workflow.
skip: The preview before 1:04 and the sponsor read at 21:48 can be skipped; the main content is valuable from 8:26 to the end.

points.h: Asking AI to coach is about being challenged, not being replaced in thinking
points.body: After being laid off from an editing and ghostwriting role at a crypto company, Katie tried agency, client-side, and freelance work, yet still felt her own ideas had hit a ceiling. Hiring a real career coach was too expensive—she estimated about $150/hour—so she switched to ChatGPT at $20/month. She didn't ask it to think for her; instead, she used it as an externalized thinking partner: explaining her situation, letting it probe and push back, especially pulling her out of herself when she tended to catastrophize. She later called this a "thinking tool." She even used it to decide whether to accept Every's column invitation—ChatGPT suggested she try it, and she's been there ever since.

points.h: Delivering to five channels alone relies on context, not typing speed
points.body: In early 2025, Katie severely overcommitted as a freelancer: within a two-week deadline, she had to deliver 8 blog posts, 3 ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts, 24 X posts, and 16 Instagram posts. She managed not by writing faster, but by what she later realized is called context engineering: first writing out the company's brand information, product details, audience, and differentiators, then letting the model generate. Building that context upfront was laborious, but once the foundation was set, production speed became very fast. She admits she repeated the overcommitment six months later—this method didn't cure her overcommitting habit.

points.h: Without foundational information, style constraints spin in neutral
points.body: On what to put in a project first, Katie is clear: not starting with rules like "use these words, avoid those" or "keep reading level low," but first giving the model a base profile of who the reader is, what their pain points are, how the product addresses them, and who the competitors and differentiators are. She says this is her instinct from writing style guides in content marketing, just now fed to AI. Only after the foundational material is in place do constraints on tone, wording, and syntax come. Her take on "style": wording issues will always nag, but without foundational information, style constraints are just spinning in neutral.

points.h: The model is the kitchen; fresh ingredients must be brought in by humans
points.body: The "data" she means isn't vague background, but first-hand material that happened after the model's knowledge cutoff or exists only in the real physical world: the company's own research, third-party reports, specific personal experiences. If you only ask the model to write a "style guide" from what it already knows, the output is commoditized information. So she assigns humans the "last mile": bringing new material the model doesn't have into the system. Her metaphor: the model is the kitchen, the process is chopping and cooking, but fresh ingredients must be carried in by a person—the quality and freshness of input ultimately determine whether a piece is worth reading.

points.h: AI as supportive technology is as powerful as when it's a production tool
points.body: Katie shared a layer she rarely discusses publicly: she has bipolar disorder, experiencing high-energy periods and facing very long lows. For her, AI's value isn't just "high output"—it's also reducing friction in daily life, making it easier for her to function as a normal person. She had put off booking a family doctor for three years, then used Codex to automatically find nearby doctors who accepted her insurance and new patients, and made the appointment. Her inbox is also pre-filtered by automation to surface only emails that truly need her reply, rather than her digging through subscription notifications every day for "bombs." Her own phrase: AI as supportive technology is just as powerful as productive technology.

points.h: A career coach isn't a single prompt; it's a project
points.body: That simple "help me as a career coach" prompt from back then has now become a standalone project in Codex: it contains her own profile and role positioning, Every's brand positioning intel, article performance data exported from the CMS, a validation folder collecting reader praise, and Q2/Q3 OKRs. Much of this material wasn't manually organized: she learned Alex Duffy's method of having AI interview her, drawing out her thoughts and organizing them into documents. She now increasingly talks to it in voice, "talking to herself," letting it prioritize, manage projects, and maintain a kanban board. She's even forgotten what's on the board, only asking when she needs a deadline for a deliverable.

points.h: Writing should be like engineering: correct each issue only once
points.body: Compound Writing started by forking Kieran's Compound Engineering: in engineering, a system should remember every piece of feedback, correct the same issue only once, and automatically do it right next time; writing should work the same. She mapped the engineering phases of brainstorming, planning, working, and reviewing onto writing's ideation, outlining, drafting, and reviewing, and designed three types of review: substantive edit for overall structure and argument, line edit for sentence-level polish, and a final publication-ready check. She no longer opens web chat windows; instead, she runs this system on Claude or ChatGPT's desktop apps, with style guides, sample articles, and other context inside, so the human only needs to bring in fresh information. The plugin was already downloadable from Every's GitHub at the time of recording.

points.h: This plugin is a gym, not a ghostwriter
points.body: She calls the plugin a gym, with the goal of making the user stronger rather than having AI ghostwrite. She breaks down favorite authors into invocable reviewer skills: Vonnegut on "start as close to the end as possible, every sentence must earn its place, give the reader a character to root for"; Hitchcock on the "bomb under the table"—if the audience sees the countdown first, a second of shock becomes five minutes of suspense. She builds these frameworks directly into the editing steps, so after writing you can invoke Vonnegut, Hitchcock, Sorkin, or Sedaris to review your draft. She believes non-professional writers benefit even more, because they don't have the baggage of "how I used to write better" blocking the way.

terms.def: An approach where AI remembers every piece of feedback, so each correction is given only once and applied automatically thereafter, making output continuously better.
A plugin that transplants compound engineering to the writing process, accumulating feedback on style, structure, and editing.
The practice of loading background information—brand, audience, competitors—into the system before asking the model to write, setting boundaries for the AI.
AI that doesn't produce content but reduces friction in life and execution, making it easier for a person to get things done.
Model Context Protocol, a common interface standard connecting models to external data and applications; Katie uses it to let small apps interact with her tools.

quotes.text: Clarity, it turns out, doesn't arrive gift wrapped from a digital assistant or even a human coach. It's something I had to dig out for myself, question by question and prompt by prompt.
But when you have that environment set up, you can just kind of run and like run fast.

So the data is the unique insight, the data point that the model doesn't have access to yet, the personal experience, all of those things that are working are ultimately going to make the writing unique.
AI is just as powerful as a supportive technology.
So compounding is the idea that every piece of feedback that you give to AI should feed back into the system to improve the next output.

if there's a bomb under the table and it explodes, that's a one moment of surprise. But if you have people sitting around the table and you show the audience the bomb under the table and say this bomb will go off in five minutes, now you have five minutes of suspense.
what I want to challenge the AI community with is thinking about how we can expand those kinds of opportunities to more people and more kinds of people in more different places.
